In [[number theory]], a '''Behrend sequence''' is an [[integer sequence]] whose multiples include [[almost all]] integers. The sequences are named after [[Felix Behrend]].

==Definition==
If <math>A</math> is a sequence of integers greater than one, and if <math>M(A)</math> denotes the set of positive integer multiples of members of <math>A</math>, then <math>A</math> is a Behrend sequence if <math>M(A)</math> has [[natural density]] one. This means that the proportion of the integers from 1 to <math>n</math> that belong to <math>M(A)</math> converges, in the limit of large <math>n</math>, to one.

==Examples==
The [[prime number]]s form a Behrend sequence, because every integer greater than one is a multiple of a prime number. More generally, a subsequence <math>A</math> of the prime numbers forms a Behrend sequence if and only if the sum of [[multiplicative inverse|reciprocal]]s of <math>A</math> diverges.{{r|rt}}

The [[semiprime]]s, the products of two prime numbers, also form a Behrend sequence. The only integers that are not multiples of a semiprime are the [[prime power]]s. But as the prime powers have density zero, their complement, the multiples of the semiprimes, have density one.{{r|rt}}

==History==
The problem of characterizing these sequence was described as "very difficult" by [[Paul Erdős]] in 1979.{{r|e}}

These sequences were named "Behrend sequences" in 1990 by Richard R. Hall, with a definition using [[logarithmic density]] in place of natural density.{{r|h}} Hall chose their name in honor of [[Felix Behrend]], who proved that for a Behrend sequence <math>A</math>, the sum of [[multiplicative inverse|reciprocal]]s of <math>A</math> must diverge.{{r|b}} Later, Hall and [[Gérald Tenenbaum]] used natural density to define Behrend sequences in place of logarithmic density.{{r|ht}} This variation in definitions makes no difference in which sequences are Behrend sequences, because the [[Davenport–Erdős theorem]] shows that, for sets of multiples, having natural density one and having logarithmic density one are equivalent.{{r|t}}

==Derived sequences==
When <math>A</math> is a Behrend sequence, one may derive another Behrend sequence by omitting from <math>A</math> any finite number of elements.{{r|ht}}

Every Behrend sequence may be decomposed into the [[disjoint union]] of infinitely many Behrend sequences.{{r|rt}}
